extracted.intended_audience: schoolmasters, university tutors, students preparing for university entrance, and parents
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on the aims and practical standards for elementary university studies and entrance examinations, especially in classical (Latin/Greek) grammar and composition, emphasizing accurate thought and disciplined study. Includes recommended exam methods, examples of good and bad candidate performance, and pedagogical advice for tutors and parents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discipline in accuracy of mind
rubrics_metrics.description: One main portion of intellectual education is to remove the original dimness of the mind’s eye; to strengthen and perfect its vision; to give the mind clearness, accuracy, precision; to enable it to use words aright, to understand what it says, to conceive justly what it thinks about, to abstract, compare, analyze, divide, define, and reason correctly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is mainly acquired by instruction that disciplines accuracy rather than by logic alone; analogy of infant vision learning to form a picture is used. Anti-pattern: hazy, misty use of grand phrases (e.g., 'large and enlightened views') shows lack of accuracy. Measure by ability to state ideas precisely and to reason clearly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grammar (elements of Latin and Greek Grammar)
rubrics_metrics.description: Grammar here means 'the art of using words properly' and comprises Orthography, Etymology, Syntax, and Prosody; for entrance it refers to the structure and characteristics of Latin and Greek, not superficial reading of many classical authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The exam should ascertain whether a student knows Etymology and Syntax, understands how sentence parts connect, peculiarities of construction, idiomatic expressions, precise meanings of terms, and the history of their formation. Do not require smattering of literature; require true scholarship in language structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Framing versus analyzing sentences (testing by translation and parsing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Translating an English sentence into Latin is the best test of a student's ability to frame (construct) a sentence; to construe and parse a passage is to analyze it and shows knowledge of Latin construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use tasks that require constructing (English→Latin) and analyzing (construe/parse) sentences. Examples provided by long tutor–candidate dialogues illustrate detailed probing (derivation, tense formation, case governance). Anti-pattern: candidate who reads widely but cannot construct or parse sentences accurately.

rubrics_metrics.name: The maxim: 'a little, but well' (focus and mastery)
rubrics_metrics.description: Students should 'get one thing well before you go on to a second'—know what you know and what you do not know; devote effort to a few things deeply rather than desultory wide reading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical steps: picture sentences as wholes, express ideas in your own words, commit important items to memory, compare and combine ideas into a coherent whole, and notice obstacles. Anti-pattern: desultory readers (like Mr. Brown) who skim many works gain curiosity but not steady mastery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual/historical/geographical knowledge behind words
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge of words must include the history and geography implied by them (e.g., understanding why Xenophon’s 'Anabasis' is an 'ascent' in relation to Persia, Sardis, Xerxes, and the seat of government).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should probe whether candidates can link lexical meanings to historical/geographical facts and explain why certain usages arose. Anti-pattern: inability to answer simple contextual questions about the texts read.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analytic knowledge of linguistic forms and idioms
rubrics_metrics.description: Students must understand parts of speech, roots, irregular verb formation, tense formation, case governance, idiomatic usages, the force of particles (e.g., nam, et), and distinctions like id quod vs quod.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exam-style probing: identify derivations (ἀναβαίνω → ἀνά + βαίνω), detect irregular verb formation (βαίνω → βήσομαι), determine what case a verb governs, and explain idiomatic constructions (venit mihi in mentem). Use specific Q&A examples to test depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Idiomatic translation and stylistic judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond literal construal, students should translate into natural, idiomatic English and exercise stylistic judgment (e.g., rendering 'Cicero Appio salutem' as 'My dear Appius' rather than a stiff literal 'Greets Appius').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess ability to choose appropriate register, convey rhetorical nuance, and explain why one English rendering is preferable to another. Test includes discussing choices and recognizing Latin stylistic devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical communicative and reasoning skills
rubrics_metrics.description: Education should enable a man to make a telling speech, write a good letter, produce sensible advice under difficulties, state an argument or a question clearly, and take a clear survey of a whole transaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the practical outcomes of accuracy and disciplined study; lack of these abilities indicates insufficient training. Exercises and examination tasks should measure applied rhetoric, letter-writing, and practical reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Steadiness, perseverance, and liking application
rubrics_metrics.description: Students should have steadiness, perseverance, and a taste for application (including subjects like logic and algebra) rather than shunning effortful thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: those who avoid logic and mathematics often lack consistency and cannot be relied on for sustained intellectual work; evaluate persistence and willingness to engage in intellectual 'gymnastics.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Entrance examinations should test depth and accuracy, not superficial breadth
rubrics_metrics.description: An Entrance Examination should aim to test the student's accurate scholarship and the particular character of the institution’s requirements, not reward mere wide reading or name-dropping of authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design exams to probe real understanding and accurate knowledge (as in the detailed viva-style examples). Tutors should advise candidates to prepare specifically for the exam’s character rather than complain about its particularity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tutor recommendation: prepare specifically and be well-grounded
rubrics_metrics.description: Tutors should counsel candidates to prepare for the examination’s particular character and to become well-grounded: better to delay residence and acquire focused preparation (e.g., six months of study) than to come ill-prepared.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural guidance: recommend targeted reading, possibly attendance at a good school or private tutoring, and emphasize focused, steady preparation rather than hurried general reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of steady, exact, and diligent study (over showy reading)
rubrics_metrics.description: Goodness, exactness, diligence, and the correct and the unexceptionable are vastly more desirable than their contraries even if less entertaining; steady careful study is superior to showy but shallow reading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a pedagogical value-criterion: reward and cultivate habits of thoroughness and correctness. Examples contrast the tediousness of steady work with the empty pleasure of facile reading.
